raw_text:
The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) has transformed prevention of sudden cardiac death since the first human implants of transvenous systems [1]. However, transvenous leads remain the “weak link,” exposing patients to pneumothorax, venous occlusion, endocarditis, lead fracture, insulation failure, difficult extraction, and systemic infection. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to preserve defibrillation efficacy while avoiding intravascular and intracardiac hardware [2]. Its generator is placed laterally, usually in an intermuscular pocket, and the parasternal electrode remains entirely extrathoracic.

Early feasibility work demonstrated reliable ventricular fibrillation detection and conversion without transvenous leads [2]. Subsequent prospective studies confirmed high conversion success and acceptable short-term safety, establishing the S-ICD as a credible alternative for patients requiring defibrillation but not chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP) [3-5]. Large registry experience further supported effectiveness in broader practice, with most complications occurring early and treatable without endovascular extraction [6]. The randomized PRAETORIAN trial was pivotal: in patients with an ICD indication but no pacing indication, S-ICD therapy was non-inferior to transvenous ICD therapy for a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [7]. The UNTOUCHED study extended reassurance to contemporary primary-prevention patients with low ejection fraction, showing low inappropriate shock rates when modern programming and sensing filters were used [8].

The main advantage of the S-ICD is anatomical. Avoiding transvenous leads is particularly attractive in young patients, those with limited venous access, inherited arrhythmia syndromes, prior device infection, hemodialysis, congenital heart disease, or anticipated long device exposure [9]. Population data show increasing adoption, although use has remained selective and influenced by operator experience, reimbursement, and patient characteristics [10]. Secondary analyses from randomized and registry cohorts suggest that lead-related complications and systemic infections are less common with S-ICD therapy, whereas pocket complications and early sensing issues remain important [11,12].

Patient selection is central. The S-ICD is inappropriate when a patient needs permanent pacing, ATP for frequent monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, or resynchronization. Conversely, it is well suited to primary-prevention patients, survivors of ventricular fibrillation, and many channelopathy or cardiomyopathy patients whose principal risk is rapid polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation. Pre-implant electrocardiographic screening is required because the S-ICD senses subcutaneous far-field signals rather than intracardiac electrograms [13]. Screening failure is more common with high body mass index, low QRS amplitude, bundle branch block, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and abnormal repolarization.

Inappropriate shocks were the major early limitation. T-wave oversensing, myopotential noise, supraventricular tachycardia, low-amplitude signals, and lead-position problems all contribute [14]. Advances have been substantial: dual-zone programming, morphology discrimination, the conditional shock zone, software updates, and the SMART Pass high-pass filter have reduced oversensing and inappropriate therapy [15,16]. Implant quality also matters. Posterior generator position, parasternal lead proximity, and avoidance of fat under the coil improve shock vector geometry; the PRAETORIAN score formalized radiographic assessment of implant position and defibrillation success probability [17,18].

Implant technique has evolved from three-incision to two-incision approaches and from subcutaneous to intermuscular generator placement. The learning curve is real: early cases have longer procedure times and more pocket and sensing issues, but outcomes improve with standardized technique and team familiarity [19]. Infection usually involves the pocket rather than the bloodstream and is often managed by complete system removal, which is technically simpler than transvenous lead extraction [20]. Comparative observational studies generally show similar survival and appropriate shock efficacy versus transvenous ICDs, with fewer lead-related complications but no ATP benefit [21].

Specific populations illustrate the device’s niche. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the S-ICD avoids lifelong transvenous lead burden, although repolarization abnormalities can increase screening failure and oversensing risk [22]. In congenital heart disease, venous anomalies, shunts, prosthetic valves, and prior surgery make extravascular defibrillation appealing [23]. Pediatric and young adult experience is favorable but requires attention to body size, growth, cosmesis, and generator discomfort [24]. In Brugada syndrome and other channelopathies, the absence of pacing need often makes the S-ICD attractive, though dynamic electrocardiographic changes can affect sensing [25].

The principal limitation remains lack of pacing. This is clinically relevant because ATP can terminate monomorphic ventricular tachycardia painlessly and reduce shocks. Some patients initially selected for an S-ICD later develop pacing indications, particularly with progressive cardiomyopathy, conduction disease, or medication-related bradycardia. Hybrid strategies are emerging: leadless pacemakers can coexist with S-ICDs, and early reports show feasible device-device interaction testing [26,27]. Future systems may integrate extravascular defibrillation, leadless pacing, ATP, and remote diagnostics more seamlessly.

In contemporary practice, the S-ICD should not be viewed as a replacement for the transvenous ICD but as a complementary platform. The best candidates are those with a clear defibrillator indication, no foreseeable pacing requirement, and elevated concern about transvenous lead complications. The transvenous ICD remains preferable when ATP, bradycardia pacing, or resynchronization is needed. Continuing improvements in sensing algorithms, implant technique, defibrillation-vector assessment, and leadless-device integration have narrowed early disadvantages [28-30]. For appropriately selected patients, the S-ICD offers durable protection from sudden death while avoiding many of the long-term hazards inherent to intravascular leads.
